description: PasswordsCon talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: Password surveys are shit!
talks.teaser: Shows how password survey questions get misread, and why people's answers about accounts and PINs fall short.
talks.summary:
Per Thorsheim, a long-time organiser of the PasswordsCon event, argues that most password surveys give unreliable answers. He traces his interest to a consulting engagement years ago, where a quick guessing exercise against a large company's domain turned up an administrator account protected by the word "password".

Most of the talk is a live audience exercise. Attendees are asked how many passwords, unique passwords and accounts they have, and the speaker shows how each question is open to interpretation. People count only the accounts they use often, leave out loyalty programmes, work systems and PINs, and rarely know how many services they have signed up for. When people are asked to list every account they have ever created, the total tends to rise several times over. He also raises PIN habits, whether spaces are allowed in passphrases, and whether respondents understand two-step verification, which many do not.

He concludes that survey results are only meaningful when the exact wording, the interview method and the respondent's understanding are recorded. He proposes a shared core question set so that results can be compared across countries, ages and groups. In the Q&A he says he recommends password managers for many people but thinks a written list kept at home can be enough for low-risk users.

talks.title: Can a password management service safely learn about users' passwords?
talks.teaser: Explores how a password manager could study user password habits while protecting individual data with privacy techniques.
talks.summary:
Jeffrey P Goldberg, who works on 1Password's research, opens with a concrete research question: is enabling two-factor authentication on a password manager linked to weaker account passwords? He explains that the company deliberately avoids collecting account password strength, so any study has to be designed so no user is put at risk. The central problem is gathering sensitive measurements from client software without exposing them.

He argues that simple anonymization is not enough. Hashed identifiers can often be reversed, and supposedly anonymous datasets can be re-identified once combined with outside data the designer does not control. He reviews privacy approaches: coarse binning of results, the random response method from survey research that encourages honest answers, and differential privacy, which adds calibrated statistical noise to limit re-identification. Homomorphic encryption and multiparty computation can compute over secrets without a trusted third party, but he says they remain too slow and complicated for practical use. A Netflix ratings case illustrates how a dataset released as anonymous was re-identified using public ratings.

The talk ends without an answer, since the research is early and the trade-offs between noise, sample size and confidence are unresolved. The practical takeaway is to assume data will leak, treat statistical error as a normal part of analysis, and design privacy guarantees in from the start. In the Q&A, an attendee suggested encrypting a one-bit strength rating for server-side comparison, which Goldberg said could be workable with existing tools.

talks.title: Your Passwords Should Be Shorter
talks.teaser: Works through the math of password length and hash cracking to argue that 15 random characters can be enough.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a joke about hacker-conference one-upmanship over password length, then makes a technical point. The bcrypt hashing function only uses the first 72 bytes of input, and multi-byte UTF-8 characters such as emoji use up that budget faster, so very long passwords can be silently cut short. Past vendor storage failures are cited as a reason not to assume large companies get this right.

To judge how long a password really needs to be, the speaker builds a threat model. The worst case is a fast MD5 hash, attacked by a cloud GPU cluster costing roughly a billion dollars a year, with a fudge factor added on top. Over an eight-year lifetime, that works out to about 85 bits of entropy, which 15 random letters and digits supply. Slower hashes such as bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2 and Argon2 widen the margin considerably, and a hardware security key is presented as a stronger defense against phishing and account takeover.

In the question period, the speaker concedes that diceware-style passphrases are a different case because people can memorize them, and notes that a password manager vendor chose a similar default length for usability reasons. Audience members warn that advice like this gets pushed to extremes, and suggest standards bodies as a channel. The takeaway: generate 15-character random passwords, and add a special character only where a system insists on one.

talks.title: Comparing Centrally and Locally Verified Memorized Secrets
talks.teaser: Explains how activation secrets for multi-factor authenticators differ from passwords in threats, limits and design.
talks.summary:
Jim Fenton, a consultant on the NIST SP 800-63 revision, opens by separating memorized secrets used to log in to a central service from activation secrets. An activation secret is the PIN or passphrase a user types to unlock a multi-factor authenticator, such as a hardware token, smart card or phone-based credential. He argues the earlier draft lumped the two together, which fit poorly, because the threats differ. Instead of cracking a breached server database, an attacker of an activation secret is more likely to combine shoulder surfing with theft of the device, or to use side channels on the hardware.

The talk then walks through design factors: length and composition, and the fact that short PINs cluster around dates and years, so extra digits add less than expected. Block lists of common values help only modestly, because attackers can see the list and simply skip those values. Throttling is central, but many standalone authenticators have no clock, so they fall back to hard lockouts after around ten failed tries. That can brick the device, which makes a backup authenticator essential. Biometrics came up in the Q&A as a complement rather than a replacement, since sensors fail with wet hands or masks.

Fenton's takeaway is that activation secrets need their own guidance, and that password rules such as long required lengths do not transfer, since many authenticators accept only a few characters. Practitioners should check each authenticator's retry limit, secret size and storage limits before relying on it. He noted that the next draft of the guidance was still subject to review.

talks.title: Passkeys: Where we started and where we're going
talks.teaser: Traces how passkeys grew out of FIDO security keys into synced, phishing-resistant credentials meant to replace passwords.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a 2009 phishing breach at Google, which the speaker gives as the reason the company committed to keeping credential phishing away from its staff. It then follows the FIDO work that came after: the U2F protocol built around removable USB security keys, the move to built-in platform authenticators such as fingerprint and face unlock, and the WebAuthn specification that lets websites use them. The speaker argues these steps improved security, but passwords stayed in place as a fallback and adoption stayed low because users had to buy and carry hardware.

Passkeys are presented as the next step. They reuse the same FIDO cryptography, but their private keys can sync between devices within one vendor's ecosystem, and they can be used across ecosystems through a proximity flow that scans a QR code and connects over Bluetooth. The speaker ran a live Android demo in which a user created a passkey during a bank login, was offered it through autofill, reused it in the bank's app, and then signed into a laptop with the phone nearby. Discoverable credentials remove the need to type usernames, and keys remain bound to the hardware.

For practitioners, the takeaways are that a passkey combines possession and user verification in a single step, that sync scope follows platform ecosystems rather than browser profiles, and that sites should plan for autofill-driven sign-in instead of relying on dedicated buttons. The session closed with an open question about how a platform should verify that a new device belongs to the same user.

talks.title: All Things FIDO (Panel + Q&A)
talks.teaser: Industry panelists discuss how FIDO standards and passkeys aim to replace passwords through better usability.
talks.summary:
The panel, held at PasswordsCon during BSides Las Vegas 2022, brought together representatives from the FIDO Alliance and major platform vendors to discuss FIDO standards and the move toward passkeys. The moderator opened by contrasting the early YubiKey pitch from over a decade ago with where the ecosystem stands now, and the panelists agreed that usability has become the main focus when it comes to reducing reliance on passwords.

Panelists described how passkeys are presented to users as a screen-lock sign-in that syncs across devices through platform providers, and how user research with an outside UX firm shaped terminology and onboarding flows. Much of the discussion covered the security trade-offs of syncing credentials through vendors rather than keeping them on a single hardware token. Account recovery after device loss, shared devices, vendor lock-in and privacy concerns around consumer federated sign-in also came up, with the speakers acknowledging that several of these problems remain open.

For developers, the speakers said platform APIs and open-source libraries reduce the implementation work, and pointed to developer resources and a community group being built out. Audience questions pressed on phishing resistance, credential cloning and revocation. The practical takeaway was that passkeys are meant to become the default for most consumers, while hardware security keys remain the recommended choice for high-assurance use cases.

talks.title: bscrypt - A Cache Hard Password Hash
talks.teaser: Introduces a password hashing function designed to resist GPU cracking through cache-hard memory lookups.
talks.summary:
Steve Thomas introduces bscrypt, a password hashing and key derivation function built on ideas from bcrypt. He sorts key stretching into computationally hard, memory hard and cache hard designs, and explains that bcrypt was cache hard by accident, because its Blowfish S-boxes were small tables that slowed down GPU attackers.

He then goes through the weaknesses that shaped the new design. These include bcrypt's mishandling of null bytes and sign-extended Unicode input, and PBKDF2's habit of rerunning its full iteration work when asked for extra output. bscrypt hashes all inputs up front with BLAKE2b, uses 64-bit operations, and performs many small random table lookups. Overlapping S-boxes let the table size be set in kilobyte steps, and the state is rotated so that bits unused in one lookup feed later ones.

Benchmarks against settings matched to a GPU attacker show PBKDF2-SHA256 taking roughly 800 milliseconds for a defender, while bscrypt needs only a few milliseconds. Tuned minimum settings can reach about one millisecond per hash while staying far beyond what GPUs can crack quickly. In questions, he noted that FPGA boards with small on-chip cache slow down as table sizes grow. Practitioners should choose a cache size above typical attacker hardware, keep hashing time near 100 milliseconds, and measure single-threaded cost, since parallel hashing reduces server throughput. The code is published on GitHub.

talks.title: Why kidz couldn't care less about your password advice.
talks.teaser: Explains why children ignore standard password advice and how streaks, gaming and sharing habits shape their security choices.
talks.summary:
Mia Landsem, an ethical hacker who also helps victims of image abuse, argues that password advice written for adults does not reach children. She opens with Norwegian survey figures on how many young people have social media profiles and gaming accounts, and how often those accounts require logins.

The central finding is that many children share passwords, mostly to keep Snapchat streaks alive or to get help from a friend or parent. She describes weak school practices, such as passwords built from names and birth years, and confusing terminology around two-step verification that children do not understand. She also argues that password managers packed with features overwhelm young users, and that gaming account takeovers and reward-driven habits are a major driver of risky behaviour. Her suggestions include simpler tools, two-step security built into streak features, small low-cost options for keeping streaks, and parents explaining consequences instead of taking phones away.

The talk closes with the stakes when shared credentials expose intimate material. She describes sextortion and non-consensual image sharing she sees in her casework. Her takeaway for practitioners is that security guidance should be standardized, easier to use, and matched to what children care about, with platforms, schools and adults sharing responsibility rather than leaving it to children.

talks.title: I know...But I Have a System
talks.teaser: Explains why staff resist password managers and how empathy and gentle onboarding can win them over.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a software tester who studies how apps can be misused, starts from the point that password managers help both individuals and companies, yet many staff never adopt them. Rolling out a licensed tool is the easy part. The gap between accounts and real use is common, and it is often widest among managers, new hires and people going through difficult periods.

The middle of the talk looks at the reasons people give for not using the tool, such as already having a personal system, having nothing important to protect, losing faith after a technical problem, or finding setup boring. Ordering people to adopt it, through policy emails and threats, usually produces minimal compliance or quiet defiance. The speaker argues for respectful listening, paid time for setup (about an hour per person), getting managers on board first, and walking people through setup step by step in person. Drop-in help sessions, a playful summer event, and storing routine shared credentials in the vault were presented as ways to build trust and peer advocates inside the organisation.

The closing takeaway is that adoption depends on people feeling safe enough to learn, and that habits can shift later during life events such as marriage, having children, illness or divorce, when people reassess their routines. Audience questions covered SSO and MFA rollout, trust in IT departments, shared accounts and audit trails. The message was to build a security culture rather than simply mandate a tool.

talks.title: Protecting Against Breached Credentials in Identity Workflows
talks.teaser: Shows how credential stuffing reaches login flows and which identity-layer controls, such as breach detection and bot defense, blunt it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at credential stuffing, the reuse of usernames and passwords exposed in unrelated breaches against live login pages. The speaker, who works on threat research at an identity platform, explains that attackers use these pairs for account takeover, then harvest personal details from compromised accounts to plan later attacks. He notes that a work email reused on a personal service can also open a path into an employer's systems. Drawing on authentication logs from many customer tenants, he separates opportunistic attackers, who use older public leaks and crude botnets, from patient ones who use fresh leaks, residential IP networks and human-like behavior.

The middle of the talk follows a real attack timeline. Breaches are often disclosed by outsiders rather than found by the victim, and leaked credentials can be added to a breach-detection workflow within minutes of being loaded. The controls discussed include breach credential checks that trigger forced resets or user education, bot detection, rate limiting, risk-based pre-login assessment and multi-factor authentication. He argues that rate limits and impossible-travel alerts miss careful attackers and privacy-minded users, and that SMS and email factors are weak, so defenses should be layered rather than relying on one control.

The audience discussion covered small organizations, where a managed provider's essentials bundle of MFA, awareness training, endpoint protection and email security is often the practical starting point. Questions also touched on whether users should be notified before an attack, with the speaker explaining that stale leaks can be irrelevant and that proactive notification is ultimately the responsibility of the company that held the data. The practical takeaway is to combine breach checks, bot defenses and strong factors, and to choose controls based on what an account protects and how much friction users will accept.

talks.title: Secrets of the Second Factor: Threat Hunting with Multi Factor Authentication
talks.teaser: Shows how to threat hunt MFA logs for rogue devices, shared phones and suspicious login reports.
talks.summary:
Susan Paskey, who writes as base 16, frames the talk for organizations rather than personal accounts and assumes two-factor authentication is already deployed. After a correct password, the second factor is the target of attacks that vendors rarely mention: repeated pushes or code guessing, help desk social engineering, phishing proxies, weak account recovery, and password dumps checked against MFA prompts.

The middle section is a hunting walkthrough. Beyond raw MFA logs, the speaker recommends pairing them with asset and application inventories, known corporate subnets, employee locations and help desk tickets. Each case starts from log fields such as the access device, IP and ASN, application, and factor result. Findings include a brute-force pattern traced to a mistyped desk phone number, a dormant account being hammered, one phone number shared by six help desk users through an extension that auto-accepted pushes, a support technician adding a phone to colleagues' accounts, and a contractor group using an employee's credentials. The speaker also cautions that IP geolocation and user-agent strings can mislead.

The closing advice is to limit self-enrollment, reconsider phone-call factors, change default prompts, and educate users to report suspicious prompts and credential-sharing requests. Contractors should be included in security training. The main message is that MFA needs continuous log review, establishing a normal baseline and investigating what falls outside it.

talks.title: The One With The Foreign Wordlist
talks.teaser: Shows how transliteration, keyboard layout mismatches and emoji substitution create wordlists for cracking non-English passwords.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that password cracking research leans heavily on English words and names, which leaves passwords built from other languages under-tested. They make the case for lean, targeted wordlists over huge general ones, since large lists waste time against slow hashes. Their advice is to keep base words simple and let hashcat rules generate the variations on the GPU.

The first technique covers transliteration. Many people type words from their own language on a Latin keyboard the way the words sound, so a Russian or Greek word may appear as a phonetic Latin spelling. The speakers ran an English dictionary through a cloud translation service to produce phonetic Latin versions for several languages, then added rules for common letter habits, such as swapping a letter for a visually similar one. A second technique covers keyboard layout mismatches. A word typed on one language's layout while the system is set to another produces what looks like random characters, which can be mapped back to real words with a small tool they built. They also presented a tool that turns words into emojis, including combinations and skin tone modifiers, and used n-gram text sources to generate phrases.

The talk closed with practical notes. Emoji passwords are increasingly common because phones make emoji entry easy, and websites may count emojis differently toward length rules. Results on public hash lists were limited, but the speakers expected better yield against corporate hashes where multiple keyboard languages are in use. The takeaway is to tailor base wordlists to the target's language and keyboard, and to rely on rules rather than bigger lists.

talks.title: Cracking passwords for good, bad & commercial purposes: second thoughts on password cracking
talks.teaser: Examines the ethics of cracking leaked passwords and a group threat model showing which attacks length and complexity actually stop.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a long-running debate at PasswordsCon about whether cracking leaked password hashes is ethical and legal. To show how much one credential can be worth, the speaker recalls a hijacked news agency account that posted a fake explosion alert and briefly moved markets. He then shares lighter research on predictable choices, including birth years, personal interests and Android unlock patterns, and argues that biometric unlock still depends on a strong PIN as a fallback.

Co-presenter Jeremy Gosney leads an audience exercise to threat model password security. The group lists threats such as physical theft of databases, malicious insiders, online brute force, keyloggers, SQL injection, phishing and remote code execution, then checks which ones length and complexity would actually stop. Most fall outside what hashing or strong choices can defend against, since an attacker with code execution or access to plaintext bypasses them. Reuse is the clear exception, and unique passwords, ideally generated by a password manager, address the widest set of threats.

The closing section covers caveats: human-chosen strength is hard to measure, a password manager's master password should rely on a slow key derivation function, and a keyed hash held in a hardware security module protects stored credentials on the service side. The session ends with a pessimistic note about the field's direction, with the expectation that standards such as FIDO2 may eventually replace passwords.
